OUTLINE VIEW

Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Identify risk factors associated with rheumatoid arthritis.
Assess how the inflammatory process of rheumatoid arthritis leads to joint destruction.
Determine the appropriate workup and diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis.
Apply the appropriate medical management for rheumatoid arthritis, including first-line drugs.
Identify manifestations of foot/ankle pathology in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (Resource
1).
Implement nonsurgical and surgical management for foot/ankle pathology in patients with
rheumatoid arthritis.

Rheumatoid arthritis is a systemic inflammatory disease of the synovium.
According to the 2010 American College of Rheumatology revised classification criteria, a
patient must score at least six points based on joint distribution, serology, symptom duration,
and presence of acute-phase reactants (Table 1). Radiographs are no longer required for
diagnosis.
Table 1 Clinical Classification of Rheumatoid Arthritis: A Scoring System

2. with the synovitis not better explained by another disease

a score of at least 6/10 is needed for classification of a patient having definite RA)c

ACPA = anticitrullinated protein antibody, ACR-EULAR = American College of Rheumatology/European League
Against Rheumatism, CRP = C-reactive protein, ESR = erythrocyte sedimentation rate, RA = rheumatoid arthritis, RF =
rheumatoid factor.
a The criteria are aimed at classification of newly presenting patients. In addition, patients with erosive disease
typical of RA with a history compatible with prior fulfillment of the 2010 criteria should be classified as having RA.
Patients with long-standing disease, including those whose disease is inactive (with or without treatment) and who,
based on retrospectively available data, have previously fulfilled the 2010 criteria should be classified as having RA.
b Differential diagnoses vary among patients with different presentations but may include conditions such as
systemic lupus erythematosus, psoriatic arthritis, and gout. If the relevant differential diagnoses to consider are
unclear, an expert rheumatologist should be consulted.
c Although patients with a score of <6/10 are not classifiable as having RA, their status can be reassessed, and the
criteria may be fulfilled cumulatively over time.
d Joint involvement refers to any swollen or tender joint on examination, which may be confirmed by imaging
evidence of synovitis. Distal interphalangeal joints, first carpometacarpal joints, and first metatarsophalangeal joints
are excluded from assessment. Categories of joint distribution are classified according to the location and number of
involved joints, with placement into the highest category possible based on the pattern of joint involvement.
e Large joints refers to shoulders, elbows, hips, knees, and ankles.
f Small joints refers to the metacarpophalangeal joints, proximal interphalangeal joints, second through fifth
metatarsophalangeal joints, thumb interphalangeal joints, and wrists.
g In this category, at least one of the involved joints must be a small joint; the other joints can include any
combination of large and additional small joints and other joints not specifically listed elsewhere (eg,
temporomandibular, acromioclavicular, sternoclavicular).
h Negative refers to International unit (IU) values that are less than or equal to the upper limit of normal (ULN) for

the laboratory and assay; low-positive refers to IU values higher than the ULN but ≤3 times the ULN for the
laboratory and assay; high-positive refers to IU values >3 times the ULN for the laboratory and assay. If RF
information is only available as positive or negative, a positive result should be scored as low-positive for RF.
i Normal/abnormal is determined by local laboratory standards.
j Duration of symptoms refers to patient self-report of the duration of signs or symptoms of synovitis (eg, pain,
swelling, tenderness) of joints that are clinically involved at the time of assessment, regardless of treatment status.
Reproduced with permission from Aletaha D, Neogi T, Silman AJ, et al: 2010 Rheumatoid arthritis classification
criteria: An American College of Rheumatology/European League Against Rheumatism collaborative initiative.
Arthritis Rheum 2010;62(9):2569-2581.
Epidemiology
Prevalence: 0.5% to 1% of the population has variation of rheumatoid arthritis.1
Prevalence increases with age, greatest in patients aged 65 to 80 years
Twice as common in females as males
More prevalent in northern latitudes than southern latitudes and urban areas versus rural
areas2
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
Periarticular bone loss

Osteology
Bone resorption typically occurs at the location at which the synovium inserts into bone,
leading to loss of subchondral bone and degeneration of cartilage. Fibroblasts and
inflammatory cells lead to osteoclast differentiation and bone loss (Figure 1).

Figure 1
AP radiograph of bilateral ankles of a patient with rheumatoid arthritis demonstrates
severe arthritis of the ankles. (Courtesy of Lew Schon, MD, Baltimore, MD.)
Cartilage
Hyperplastic synovium destroys cartilage.

Cartilage
Hyperplastic synovium directly invades and adheres to the cartilage, causing damage.
Matrix metalloproteinases further promote degradation of cartilage.
Vascular Anatomy
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:02 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001016
5/20

Increased angiogenesis

Vascular Anatomy
Increased angiogenesis in the synovium leads to increased release of cytokines,
chemokines, and growth factors.
Nerves
Peripheral neuropathy
Sensory or sensorimotor neuropathy affects 33% to 75% of patients with rheumatoid
arthritis.3
Tarsal tunnel syndrome
Interdigital neuromas
Joints and Ligaments
Hyperplastic synovium
Abnormal proliferation of fibroblast-like synoviocytes leads to hyperplastic synovium.
Cervical instability
90% of patients with rheumatoid arthritis have cervical instability. Most common is
atlantoaxial subluxation, followed by basilar invagination and subaxial subluxation.
Dorsal dislocation of lesser metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joints
Skin
Rheumatoid nodules: firm, nontender, moveable masses as large as 5 cm

Skin
Rheumatoid nodules often occur on extensor surfaces and areas of increased pressure,
such as the medial and lateral malleoli and the medial and lateral eminences of the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:02 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001016
6/20

forefoot. The nodules consist of granulation tissue and inflammatory cells in a palisading
pattern and central area of fibrinoid necrosis4 (Figure 2).
Figure 2
Clinical photograph of a foot shows a rheumatoid nodule on the plantar forefoot.
(Courtesy of Lew Schon, MD, Baltimore, MD.)
Tendons
Tenosynovitis and tendon rupture
Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction
Etiology
Two subtypes: with and without anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPAs)
Genetic cause
Monozygotic twins have a concordance rate of 15% to 30%, whereas dizygotic twins have a
concordance rate of only 5%.
Human leukocyte antigen-DR4, human leukocyte antigen-DR1
Environmental causes
Interaction between human leukocyte antigen-DR1 genes and environment
Smoking
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:02 PM
AAOS | Rheumatoid Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001016
7/20

Bacteria
Viruses

Etiology
ACPA is the result of an abnormal antibody response to a range of citrullinated proteins,
including fibrin, vimentin, fibronectin, Epstein-Barr nuclear antigen 1, alpha-enolase,
type II collagen, and histones, all of which are distributed throughout the entire body.5
ACPAs are detected in 67% of patients with rheumatoid arthritis. ACPA-positive patients
have more aggressive disease.
Smoking may alter the bacterial flora of the mouth and lung, whereas diet and antibiotic
agents may alter the gut flora, contributing to rheumatoid arthritis. Epstein-Barr virus
and parvovirus B19 have been associated with triggering rheumatoid arthritis.
Natural History
Triggering stage
Environmental risk factors trigger ACPA production. Examples of triggers include noxious
agents, such as smoke and silica dust, infections, such as Porphyromonas gingivalis,
Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, and Epstein-Barr virus.5 Smoking is the most
common trigger.
Maturation stage
During this stage, ACPA titers gradually increase. This stage may last several years before
onset of joint symptoms.
Targeting stage
The synovium of joints is infiltrated by immune cells that produce an inflammatory response
led by fibroblast-like synoviocytes.
Fulminant stage
Abnormal proliferation of fibroblast-like synoviocytes and resistance to apoptosis leads to
hyperplastic synovium.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:02 PM
AAOS | Rheumatoid Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001016
8/20

Risk Factors
Female sex
Family history of rheumatoid arthritis
Age, most commonly 65 to 80 years
Exposure to tobacco smoke

Risk Factors
Other risk factors include exposure to occupational dust (silica) and air pollution, obesity,
and low vitamin D intake and levels. A decreased risk is associated with fish and omega-3
fatty acid consumption, moderate alcohol intake, healthy diet, statin use, and oral
contraceptive/hormone replacement.6
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Morning stiffness, pain in multiple joints (commonly symmetric small joints)
Most commonly affects hands and feet
Initially, the most commonly affected joints are the metacarpophalangeal, proximal
interphalangeal, wrist, and MTP joints. May first present in the forefoot before any findings
are noted in the hand.
Long-term foot deformity is present in as many as 90% of patients.7
Joint swelling (most prominent in small joints of the hands and feet)
Physical Examination
Rheumatoid nodules are firm nodules in the soft tissue as large as 5 cm, most commonly over
the dorsal foot and areas of pressure, such as the malleoli and medial/lateral forefoot (Figure
3).

Figure 3
Clinical photograph of a foot shows a rheumatoid nodule on the plantar aspect of the medial
forefoot. (Courtesy of Lew Schon, MD, Baltimore, MD.)
Hand deformities: metacarpophalangeal joint, subluxation, ulnar drift of the fingers, swan-
neck deformity, boutonnière deformity
Foot deformities: hallux valgus (most common), claw toes, MTP subluxation (Figure 4)
Isolated talonavicular joint arthritis is associated with rheumatoid arthritis.

the metatarsophalangeal joints with associated claw toe deformity. (Courtesy of Lew Schon,
MD, Baltimore, MD.)
Neurovascular Examination
Patients may have sensory and motor deficits.
Peripheral neuropathy in as many as 75% of patients with rheumatoid arthritis
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Bilateral arthritis
Periarticular osteopenia (Figure 5)
Figure 5
Images of a knee show rheumatoid arthritis. A, AP radiograph demonstrates a subchondral
cyst in the proximal tibia with narrowing of the medial compartment of the knee. B, Sagittal
T1-weighted MRI shows a large subchondral lesion in the distal femur and proximal tibia and
an erosion on the tibial condylar surface. C, Sagittal T2-weighted MRI shows a large erosion on
the distal femur and proximal tibia, an effusion, and diffuse synovial thickening. (Reproduced
from Frassica FJ: Metabolic bone and inflammatory joint disease, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS
Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2020, pp 1642-1654.)
Juxta-articular erosions
Joint space narrowing

Computed Tomography
Preoperative planning to evaluate for deformity, bone loss, alignment (on weight-bearing CT
scans)
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Evaluate for bone marrow edema, an early sign in rheumatoid arthritis before arthritis
development.
Synovitis, joint effusion, tenosynovitis, early articular damage and bony erosions, tendon tears
Ultrasonography
Evaluate for synovitis, joint effusion, tenosynovitis, and tendon tears.
Dynamic examination: tendon subluxation, impingement
Bone Scintigraphy and Positron Emission Tomography
Limited role
Pathology
Autoimmune inflammatory response
Angiogenesis leads to increased cell migration to synovium.
Cytokines stimulate synovitis and hypertrophic synovium.
Fibroblast-like synoviocytes in synovium invade cartilage and tendon, stimulating osteoclast
activation.
Hypertrophic synovium destroys bone and cartilage.

Pathology
T cells constitute 50% of the cells in the synovium of patients with rheumatoid arthritis. T
cells recognize various native antigens, such as type II collagen, and begin an
inflammatory response by generating autoantibodies by B cells and activation helper T
cells. ACPAs contribute to inflammatory cytokine production.8 Antibodies to
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:02 PM
AAOS | Rheumatoid Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001016
12/20

immunoglobulin G called rheumatoid factors initiate a proliferative response, including
interleukin (IL)-2 secretion. Cytokines and chemokines in the synovium that contribute to
the inflammatory response include IL-1, IL-6, IL-10, IL-15, IL-12, tumor necrosis factor
(TNF), granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor, macrophage colony-
stimulating factor, and transforming growth factor.9
Diagnosis
Laboratory features
Anti- cyclic citrullinated peptide: most sensitive and specific test
Rheumatoid factor: targets Fc portion of immunoglobulin G. Approximately 90% of patients
are positive for rheumatoid factor.
Elevation of acute-phase reactants: erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein level
Joint fluid analysis: decrease complement, elevated rheumatoid factor levels
2010 diagnostic criteria: score greater than or equal to 6 out of 1010 (Table 1)
Differential Diagnosis
Infection
Osteoarthritis
Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction
Seronegative spondyloarthropathy11
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Pharmacologic Management
NSAIDs
Steroids
Prednisone
Nonbiologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs)
Methotrexate (current preferred treatment option)
Others (leflunomide, sulfasalazine, chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:02 PM
AAOS | Rheumatoid Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001016
13/20

Biologic DMARDs
Etanercept (TNF-α receptor linked to immunoglobulin; binds and inhibits TNF receptor)
Infliximab (chimeric monoclonal antibody to TNF-α)
Rituximab (monoclonal antibody to cluster of differentiation 20 antigen; inhibits B cells)
Anakinra (IL-1 receptor agonist; inhibits IL-1)
Tocilizumab (monoclonal antibody to IL-6 receptor; blocks IL-6)
Abatacept (cluster of differentiation 80/86 or cluster of differentiation 27 inhibitor; results in
decreased T cell proliferation)
Tofacitinib, baricitinib (Janus kinase inhibitor; blocks tyrosine kinases critical to signal
transduction for IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, IL-21)
Orthopaedic Management
Management of underlying arthritis, foot/ankle deformity, tendonitis, synovitis
Physical therapy: maintain/gain motion, strength, balance
Steroid injections: temporary relief of synovitis and arthritis pain
Bracing
Bracing provides support in patients with arthritis or deformities. A solid ankle-foot orthosis
or an Arizona ankle-foot orthosis may provide support for ankle deformities.
Orthotics
Orthotics may offload areas of increased pressure, such as the metatarsal heads. This
typically is done with a metatarsal pad. Orthotics also can provide support. Also may
consider an extra-depth accommodative shoe with a rocker-bottom sole. Custom orthotics
with a medial wedge or University of California Berkeley Laboratories shoe insert orthosis
may provide increased support in patients with posterior tibial tendon dysfunction.
Surgical Management
Indications
Failed nonsurgical orthopaedic management
Goals are to relieve pain, correct deformity, restore function.
Forefoot
Plantar forefoot pain from lesser MTP dislocation: first MTP fusion and resection of lesser
metatarsal heads
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:02 PM
AAOS | Rheumatoid Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001016
14/20

Hallux valgus: first MTP fusion; hallux valgus correction is contraindicated because of
instability (Figure 6).
Patients with rheumatoid arthritis well controlled with DMARDs and no arthritis.
Consider joint-sparing procedure.
Hallux valgus: corrective osteotomy (ie, crescentic proximal osteotomy, biplanar osteotomy)
MTP dislocation: metatarsal shortening osteotomy (Weil shortening osteotomy or
metatarsal shaft shortening osteotomy)
Figure 6
AP bilateral foot and ankle radiograph demonstrates bilateral metatarsophalangeal fusions
and lesser metatarsal head resections for severe forefoot deformity caused by rheumatoid
arthritis. (Reproduced from Thomson AB, Easley ME, Boyette DM: Arthritides of the foot and
ankle, in Boyer MI, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2014, pp 1499-1509.)
Midfoot
Talonavicular arthritis: talonavicular fusion
Tarsometatarsal arthritis: tarsometatarsal fusion
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:02 PM
AAOS | Rheumatoid Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001016
15/20

Hindfoot arthritis: subtalar arthrodesis
Ankle arthritis: ankle replacement or ankle fusion
Patients with rheumatoid arthritis may have improved outcomes with ankle replacement
because of low demand and multiple joint arthritis.
Consider preoperative injections to determine which joints (subtalar, tibiotalar,
tibiotalocalcaneal) are more symptomatic.
Preoperative Assessment
Evaluate for cervical spine involvement of rheumatoid arthritis.
Pharmacologic Planning
Discontinue or limit prednisone to less than 15 mg daily.
Continue nonbiologic DMARDs.
Discontinue biologic DMARDs and wait the length of the dosing cycle (etanercept/adalimumab,
2 weeks; rituximab, 7 months prior).
Infliximab levels lowest 2 weeks before next infusion
Methotrexate, sulfasalazine, and hydroxychloroquine do not need to be discontinued.
Complications
Increased Infection Risk
Nonbiologic DMARDs do not increase postoperative risks in patients who undergo foot and
ankle surgery.12
Delayed Wound Healing
As many as 21% of patients with rheumatoid arthritis experience delayed wound healing. Risk
factors associated with delayed wound healing in patients with rheumatoid arthritis include
increased operating room time, number of incisions, and number of toes being surgically
managed.13
Nonunion/Malunion
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:02 PM
AAOS | Rheumatoid Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001016
16/20

Nonunion/malunion is possible.
Outcomes
Comparable outcomes to patients without rheumatoid arthritis
Joint-sparing procedures in patients with well-controlled rheumatoid arthritis result in superior
outcomes compared with joint resection arthroplasty in patients with hallux valgus and MTP
dislocations.

Outcomes
Nash et al14 reported satisfaction in 85% to 96% of patients after first MTP fusion.
Coughlin15 examined patients after first MTP fusion and resection of the lesser
metatarsal heads and found a 7% dislocation rate postoperatively compared with a 70%
rate preoperatively. No poor results were reported at 6-year follow-up. Ankle
replacement in patients with rheumatoid arthritis is associated with a survivorship rate
of 93% at 8.3 years postoperatively.16
Horita et al17 studied 18 feet that underwent joint-sparing correction of hallux valgus
and MTP dislocations via corrective osteotomies and demonstrated satisfactory clinical
outcomes with a mean Japanese Society of Surgery of the Foot score improvement from
62.2 to 90.8 and a 6% recurrence of deformities. In a retrospective study of 23 feet with
28 months follow-up, Fukushi et al18 compared joint-sparing corrective osteotomies to
resection arthroplasty (with first MTP fusion) and reported increased improvement in the
joint-sparing group compared with the resection arthroplasty group. Shimomura et al19
performed a similar retrospective study in 40 patients and reported no difference in self-
administered foot evaluation questionnaire clinical scores between joint-sparing
correction and resection arthroplasty at 1 year postoperatively; however, clinical
outcomes improved more quickly in the joint-sparing group.
